title: Wildcard Matching
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
p contains only lowercase English letters, '?' and '*'
notes:
## Intuition

Each `*` can swallow anywhere from zero to all remaining characters, so trying every choice by recursion explodes. But the only question that ever matters is "does the first `i` characters of `s` match the first `j` characters of `p`?". There are only (m + 1)(n + 1) such questions, and each one follows from neighbours that are one character shorter, which is a two-sequence DP like edit distance.

## Approach

1. Let row `prev` answer the question for the empty prefix of `s`: `prev[0]` is `true`, and `prev[j]` stays `true` only while the pattern prefix is all stars.
2. For each `i` from 1 to `m`, build a fresh row `curr` (all `false`; a non-empty `s` prefix never matches an empty pattern).
3. If `p[j - 1]` is `*`: either the star matches nothing (`curr[j - 1]`) or it also takes `s[i - 1]` and keeps going (`prev[j]`).
4. If it is `?` or the same letter as `s[i - 1]`, both characters pair up and the answer is `prev[j - 1]`. Any other letter leaves `false`.
5. Move to the next row with `prev = curr`. The answer is `prev[n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aa"`, `p = "a"`. The first row is `prev = [true, false]`. For `i = 1`, `p[0]` equals `s[0]`, so `curr[1] = prev[0] = true` and `prev = [false, true]`. For `i = 2`, the letters match again but `curr[1] = prev[0] = false`, so `prev = [false, false]` and the answer is `false`: one `a` cannot cover two.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n), one constant-time step per pair of prefixes.
- Space: O(n), only two rows of the table are kept.

## Pitfalls

- An empty `s` still matches a pattern made only of stars; the first row must handle that.
- `?` needs exactly one character; it never matches the empty string.
- For a star, `prev[j]` (take one more character) is what lets it absorb a long run; using `prev[j - 1]` instead makes it eat exactly one.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m`, `n` | lengths of `s` and `p` |
| `prev` | row for the first `i - 1` characters of `s`: `prev[j]` says whether they match `p`'s first `j` |
| `curr` | the same row for the first `i` characters |
| `i`, `j` | lengths of the current prefixes of `s` and `p` |

narration.4: Row for the empty prefix of s: one entry per prefix length of p.
narration.5: The empty string matches the empty pattern.
narration.6: Fill the rest of the first row, one pattern character at a time.
narration.7: An empty s only matches a pattern prefix made entirely of stars.
narration.9: Add the characters of s one at a time.
narration.10: Start the new row as all false; a non-empty prefix never matches an empty pattern.
narration.11: Try every prefix length of the pattern.
narration.12: Is the last pattern character a star?
narration.13: The star either matches nothing (left cell) or also takes s[i - 1] (cell above).
narration.14: Otherwise the last characters must pair up: '?' or the same letter.
narration.15: They do, so the answer is whatever the two shorter prefixes gave.
narration.18: This row becomes the previous row for the next character of s.
narration.20: The last cell tells whether all of s matches all of p.
